meta.title: Romanian B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1,000 more words, none of them in A1 or A2 · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Romanian → English (see the Romanian, recall the meaning) and English → Romanian (see an English meaning, recall the Romanian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling where the language is spoken, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences, events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be — no openly licensed graded word list for Romanian was found to build it from. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 513 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and careers, education, the media and technology, the environment, society and public life, law and crime, health and lifestyle, relationships, feelings and character, giving opinions and arguing a point, the linking words that join sentences into a text, travel and what goes wrong on it, services, money and housing, culture and the arts, abstract ideas, and the verbs of thinking, communicating and changing things — and the other 487 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Romanian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword carries its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own, because Romanian does not write where the stress falls. Verbs are given in the dictionary's form, with the infinitive's a (a face, to do). The 576 nouns show their gender — masculine, feminine or neuter, the neuter being masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural — their plural, and their definite form, the article being a suffix (casă, a house; casa, the house); the 237 verbs show their first person, past participle and subjunctive, and behind the All forms fold their present, imperfect, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 928 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 777 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
